title: Zionist youth and the road to Palestine in Drohiczyn
summary: The records point to a lively range of Zionist organizations and youth movements, revealing how political ideals shaped young people’s choices and community activity.

editorialContent:
![Drohiczyn on the Bug River](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4f/Drohiczyn_Zesp%C3%B3%C5%82_klasztorny_jezuit%C3%B3w_06.jpg/1920px-Drohiczyn_Zesp%C3%B3%C5%82_klasztorny_jezuit%C3%B3w_06.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=api&utm_content=thumbnail)

## A town divided—and energized

In interwar Drohiczyn, Zionism was not a single party or a shared program. It was a crowded field of organizations, arguments and youth groups, all addressing a pressing question: how could Jewish life be secured, and what should the community do about the Land of Israel? The memorial book remembers these organizations not as abstractions but as part of the town’s everyday political and social life.

Its account places the [General Zionists](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_991f50022322b636cd3bfa29), [Mizrahi](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_f7e9dee49bc7b5fe962f3fb6), [Ichud](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_22982838484b508c3ab7b007), [HeHalutz](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_33ad03fb2209f44c2a0e547c), [Hashomer Hatzair](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_90580d9772488f5f0b7b1e82) and [Poale Zion](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_eb4d2fd61b62a7d62e8add11) within the same local landscape. Their different political and religious emphases mattered, but so did the practical work of organizing: sustaining groups, teaching young people, collecting money and helping would-be pioneers prepare for migration.

The book’s terminology and passages do not always make the organizational relationships fully clear. It identifies both a General Zionist organization led by Shlomo Zelig Goldman and a separate organization called Ichud, where Goldman worked as secretary. They should not be collapsed into one body: the surviving references describe distinct names and roles, without explaining their precise relationship. The memorial record also identifies Shlomo-Zelig as a son in the Goldman family caption, but that alone does not establish further details of his organizational career.

## Betar and competing visions for youth

Among the movements remembered was [Betar](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_a6d6648cad7426296e86523d), associated in the book with Brit Trumpeldor and Revisionist Zionism. Two local members are named: [Abraham Bezdzhezsky](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_42f8f19d6932ab56f70a093a) and [Isaac Bezdzhezsky](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_38ac9745a3f740f27b47ba21), brothers identified as sons of Moshe and Hannah. The memorial book gives the town’s youth organizations a human scale: movements were not only labels in a political contest, but affiliations that shaped the lives of young people and their families.

The wider history clarifies Betar’s place in the movement. It began in Riga in 1923 as a Revisionist Zionist youth organization associated with [Ze’ev Jabotinsky](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_9b07b7b4e10425fc11223a74) and Joseph Trumpeldor. In Poland, Betar became part of a broad landscape of Zionist youth organizing. This context helps explain why the name appears in Drohiczyn, but it cannot tell us exactly what local members did at meetings or how they experienced the movement. Those details must come from the town’s own testimony, where available—not be assumed from the national history.

The memorial book also remembers religious Zionist organization through Mizrahi and records socialist Zionist currents through Poale Zion and Hashomer Hatzair. These names point to different ideas about Jewish society, religious life, labor and settlement. The evidence supplied here does not describe a complete local program for every group, so it would be misleading to assign each one specific activities in Drohiczyn without further testimony. Still, their coexistence shows that the aspiration to Palestine did not erase disagreement: it gave competing movements a shared destination around which they could organize.

## Fundraising, committees and migration

The [Drohiczyn Zionist Committee](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_555e02d3ce173af28443b640) appears in the memorial record as a body soliciting donations for pioneers from the town. Among its named members are Tzvi Ari Eizenshtein, Shmuel Fishman, Tzvi Shkolnik, Zelig Shakhat, Yehuda Zilberstein, Gdalya Kaplan, Miriam Weissman, Tzvia Waldman and Y. Roshinski. Their list is evidence of organized local effort, though it does not by itself reveal how much was raised, who received assistance or when individual contributions were made.

The book’s references to money collected for the Land of Israel place fundraising alongside political organization. Zionist work was not only debate over ideas; it required practical support for migration and settlement. The names attached to the committee suggest that this work involved both men and women. The surviving account, however, does not provide enough information to reconstruct each person’s responsibilities or the committee’s full membership.

The memorial records name people who reached or lived in the Land of Israel: Menachem Reichman, Mordechai Yudavski, Zvi Schwartz, Shaynke Feldman, Hershl Chaim, Hashe Levin and Shmuel Epelboim are described as having migrated there. Selde Goldberg is recorded as having died there; Hannah and Leah Panaberia as having lived there. These brief entries preserve routes and outcomes, but they leave questions—when each person left, by what route, and whether family accompanied them. The [Land of Israel](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_04977b79d88df9bf56e72d6b) was both a collective ideal and a destination reached through individual lives, whose histories require further research.

The book’s account of the community’s migration efforts belongs to a much larger history of Jewish emigration and settlement. But no general history can fill in the gaps in these people’s stories. In particular, the memorial record should not be treated as a complete register of everyone who left Drohiczyn: survivors compiled it from what they knew and remembered, while other relatives may appear only in migration or family archives.

## What the wider record can—and cannot—confirm

The independent records located here help establish broader context, while offering only limited confirmation of Drohiczyn’s local organizations. The [Yad Vashem Encyclopedia of the Ghettos entry for Drohiczyn](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=258) provides a separate historical reference for the town in the Holocaust period, but it does not verify the committee’s membership or the individual migration details listed in the memorial book. A general account of Betar likewise supplies the movement’s origins and Revisionist setting, not proof of particular activities in Drohiczyn.

That distinction matters. The memorial book tells us what the community chose to preserve about its Zionist currents and the people who carried them. Independent sources help situate those memories, but the available material does not independently establish the local committee’s work or confirm the individual family connections and destinations. Those remain valuable questions for future research, especially through immigration, family and organizational records.

For the [Drohiczyn Jewish community](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_39d23dc1ff780fc5e0705ad8), the road to Palestine was therefore many roads: political, educational and practical, shaped by parties and youth groups, by fundraising and by people who departed. The memorial book preserves a community reaching toward a future elsewhere, while also leaving open the intimate histories that would make that journey more complete.
